prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength concept to measurement uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The opening ballots show that seven of eight members propose exactly the same two names for B059, which tells us the attribution is not in dispute. On the science, the optical lattice clock is a case where a simple, surprising idea (trap many atoms at the magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels) was turned into an instrument whose accuracy has been checked by several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE). It resolves gravitational time dilation over millimetres, constrains drifts of fundamental constants and is the basis for the discussion of redefining the second. Theory and experiment agree closely, which I value more than anything else in a candidate. It is also a discovery about where quantum control of many atoms can be pushed, not only a technology. The redefinition of the second gives the timing a natural point of maturity.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that the committee has recently honoured the frequency comb (2005) and ion-trap quantum control and clocks (2012), so a clock prize could look like a third helping of precision metrology rather than a new discovery. A second reservation is that much of the impact is still prospective (redefinition not yet decided, geodesy and dark-matter searches not yet delivering a result), and that Lemonde, Gill, Bloom and others made real contributions that two names cannot reflect. I also recognise that I rank this first partly because it lies in my own field, where I may overvalue elegance of precision.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B059 fifth, accepts the Katori and Ye pairing as compact, but notes that Hall and Hansch (2005) and Wineland (2012) were honoured before and that Ye has links to the comb work already recognised, and puts IceCube first as a new observational window.
responses.response: I agree that overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the real test, and I would put it in the citation: the lattice clock rests on the comb but is a separate achievement, since the magic-wavelength condition and the many-atom interrogation are what delivered 10^-18 and are not in the comb or single-ion prizes. Ye's comb work is a part of his career, not of the cited achievement. Where I differ is on IceCube. The diffuse flux is solid, but I share your own worry that credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers is not clear, and as a non-specialist I cannot judge it better. I would rather credit a clean attribution than a larger instrument.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clean demonstration of quantum physics made controllable, reproduced widely, and a natural next step after the 2025 prize, while ranking B059 fourth as mature but not urgent.
responses.response: I rank circuit QED third and see its quality, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes me hesitant: two consecutive prizes for the same platform would be hard to defend, and the credit question (Girvin, Devoret and the Yale and Delft overlap) is truly open. You call the clock timing 'reasonable but not urgent'. I would answer that it is exactly the maturity we look for, because independent clocks agree at the 10^-18 level and that cannot be said for most candidates. I accept that if the committee wants a quantum-information prize, B013 is the strongest, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because a quantitative band-theory prediction was confirmed by experiment and opened a tunable platform of correlated matter, and sees B059 as important but partly outside his area.
responses.response: The prediction followed by experiment is the pattern I admire too, and I do not dismiss the field. Yet the origin of the superconductivity is still debated by your own account, and the first experimental authors (Cao and Fatemi) lie outside the three credited names, which I find a real fairness gap. I defer to you and Mehlig on condensed matter, but I cannot place moire matter above a result that has been reproduced and where the interpretation is not in doubt. If the committee thinks the field is mature enough, I would want to hear how you handle the pairing question.

responses.point: Kroll also ranks B059 first and stresses the independent confirmation from many groups and the clean two-name configuration, while admitting uncertainty about how other lattice-clock contributors would be weighed.
responses.response: I agree with the core of your case and with the doubt. I would add that the committee should check whether Katori's proposal and early Sr demonstrations and Ye's accuracy and many-body-clock work are two distinct contributions, since the citation should describe a concept plus a realisation to the frontier, not simply a better clock. I do not think the contributions of Lemonde, Gill or Bloom are a reason for adding a third name, because the concept and the record-setting realisation are well separated between the two candidates.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as supporting maturity or as a sign that the main impact is still to come.

How to weigh contributions of other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Gill, Bloom) against the two-name configuration; I know the history of this field less precisely than that of atomic structure theory.
My own assessment of moire matter and topological insulators rests on deference to condensed-matter colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates in B059. I have worked closely with the Lund attosecond group (L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate) and with Keller's group, but neither is a candidate on this shortlist. I have no known connection with Katori or Ye, and I am an atomic theorist in the same broad community, so I note that general closeness for transparency.
